t: Check Adjacent Digit Differences — Linear Scan
o:
**Understanding the problem**

Given a digit string `s`, return `true` iff every neighboring pair of digits differs by at most 2 in absolute value.

- Example 1: `"132"` — pairs give |1−3|=2 and |3−2|=1, both ≤ 2 → true.
- Example 2: `"129"` — |2−9|=7 > 2 → false.

Length is at most 100, so a single pass comparing consecutive characters is trivially sufficient. Note digits are characters; convert with `c - '0'` (or rely on character arithmetic, since `'0'..'9'` are contiguous in ASCII/Unicode).
k: A single left-to-right scan checking abs(s[i] − s[i+1]) ≤ 2 suffices.
Digit characters are ordered contiguously, so subtracting '0' converts safely (or compare characters directly).
Strings of length 2 have exactly one pair to check; there is no empty-pair edge case given constraints.

a.i: Iterate over adjacent pairs; the moment any pair exceeds difference 2, return false. If the loop completes, return true. Early exit makes the common failure case fast.
s: For i from 0 to len−2, compute abs(s[i] − s[i+1]).
If any difference exceeds 2, return false immediately.
Otherwise return true after the loop.
a.t: O(n) — one comparison per adjacent pair, with early exit on violation.
a.sp: O(1) — only loop state is used.

a.n: Approach 2: Convert to Integer Array First
a.i: Map the string to an integer array, then verify pairwise differences with a stream/every-style check. Functionally identical, slightly more allocation, but reads cleanly and generalizes if digits later need arithmetic beyond simple differences.
s: Convert each character of s to its numeric digit value.
Verify every consecutive pair satisfies abs(diff) ≤ 2 using an all/every construct.
a.t: O(n) — one conversion pass plus one verification pass.
a.sp: O(n) for the auxiliary digit array.

w:
**Wrap-up**

Use Approach 1 in an interview — it is the minimal, allocation-free solution. Pitfalls: forgetting the absolute value (checking signed differences), iterating out of bounds (`i < s.length()` instead of `i + 1 < s.length()`), and unnecessary `parseInt` of the whole string. Edge cases: length-2 strings (single pair), constant strings like `"777"` (always true), and extremes like `"09"` (difference 9 → false). Follow-ups: what threshold `k` instead of 2? What about circular adjacency (also compare first and last characters)? Both are one-line modifications of the same scan.
